## 2026-09-19 — Evidence-grade GovCon sweep: cross-source failure semantics and false-eligibility traps

### leog25/govcon-cli — WATCH — 22/30
- URL: https://github.com/leog25/govcon-cli
- Exact revision: `bf625bfe79eeaf0e351eff253ac8ab6d0396edbf`
- Date inspected: 2026-09-19
- Category: Repository / Reusable Component
- Concrete capability: MIT Python CLI/Claude skill that normalizes procurement opportunities from U.S. SAM.gov and CanadaBuys into one model, with local caching, resumable attachment downloads, bounded rate limiting, source-health metadata, source-specific pagination/truncation handling and explicit partial-source failures.
- Rare / undernoticed value: Its useful contribution is not another SAM search surface but the error/completeness contract. Source fan-out can return usable results while preserving per-source errors, every-source failure becomes `source_unavailable`, SAM query results expose a truncation flag when the upstream hard ceiling is encountered, attachment detail failures leave a lite opportunity record instead of silently deleting the opportunity, and CanadaBuys can stream very large CSV feeds into a local SQLite index.
- Buyer / painful problem: GovCon research and capture tools need to distinguish “no opportunity found” from partial/truncated/degraded upstream coverage and still retain source-specific evidence when one provider fails.
- Monetization / first paid wedge: Embed its failure-state pattern into CaptureBrief’s acquisition layer; sell a reliability/readiness tier that shows which sources were healthy, partial, truncated or unavailable before a recommendation is generated.
- Build-time / data advantage: Moderate-high; several weeks to 1–2 months of cross-source normalization, rate-limit/cache, large-file and partial-failure handling.
- Evidence inspected: exact revision and recent commit history; root README; `src/govcon_cli/adapters/sam.py` including source error accumulation, `truncated` metadata, attachment filtering, SAM “what’s new” paging, source-health count and preservation of lite records when detail enrichment fails; root MIT `LICENSE`.
- Actual public license / rights: MIT. User’s standing separate commercial-permission assertion independently applies to repository-owned code/content. SAM.gov and CanadaBuys endpoints/data retain their own access, rate and data-use terms.
- Reuse classification: Reusable, but the SAM path uses an undocumented/public-frontend JSON surface and therefore should not replace official SAM APIs for evidence authority.
- Score: A3 / B3 / C4 / D3 / E4 / F5 = **22/30**.
- Combination opportunities: Put its `healthy / partial / truncated / unavailable` semantics around `market-map`, `GSA/srt-fbo-scraper`, Sentinel packet acquisition and SLED collectors. Do not use it as the canonical federal identity/award source.
- Next action: Recreate the failure-state contract in CaptureBrief and benchmark intentionally truncated and one-source-down cases; no further generic wrapper work unless a new commit adds authoritative amendment/IDV semantics.

### UziLoogies/SAM.GOV_SCANNER — REJECT / FALSE-ELIGIBILITY RISK — 17/30
- URL: https://github.com/UziLoogies/SAM.GOV_SCANNER
- Exact revision: `d49f63a939eab9d994cf02f73d6f627841b3be1b`
- Date inspected: 2026-09-19
- Category: Repository / Negative Training Example
- What it contains: Broad local-first Rust/Tauri GovCon application with SAM ingestion, document parsing, company profiles, audit/export, subcontractor discovery and an 11-subscore opportunity scoring engine.
- Why rejected for evidence-grade use: Deep source inspection found set-aside and subcontractor compatibility scores driven by substring/fuzzy matches against certification/business-type strings. The geography path can assign a same-state-style score from place-of-performance presence without proving the contractor location match, and NAICS/certification heuristics can produce confidence-like numbers without establishing legal eligibility. These are UX heuristics only, not deterministic procurement qualification.
- Evidence inspected: `src-tauri/src/scoring.rs` and `src-tauri/src/subcontractor.rs`; README architecture/data model. The latter carries a similarly-situated assessment concept but the scoring path does not prove SBA similarly-situated requirements.
- Actual public license / rights: README says Private / All rights reserved. Per the user’s standing assertion, repository-owned code/content is treated as separately commercially permitted. That does not convert external SAM/SBA data or legal rules into repository-owned material.
- Score: A3 / B3 / C3 / D2 / E2 / F4 = **17/30**.
- Combination lesson: Add a negative regression case to CaptureBrief: fuzzy certification/business-type text may suggest review candidates but must never establish set-aside, certification or similarly-situated eligibility.
- Next action: Do not use its scoring outputs as eligibility truth; retain only the clean-room failure cases and local-first product ideas.

## 2026-09-19 — Permit/public-data and procurement data-engine sweep

### PermitStack/permitstack-typescript — STRONG / MASTER REFERRAL — 26/30
- URL: https://github.com/PermitStack/permitstack-typescript
- Exact revision: `b3cedac75a5b8d84a52f567a09b1b2314841081b`
- Date inspected: 2026-09-19
- Category: Dataset/API / Reusable Component / Business Opportunity
- Concrete capability: Generated TypeScript SDK/OpenAPI surface over a hosted U.S. building-permit corpus. The current repository/commit lineage reports roughly 102M+ permits, 10,000+ cities and 48 states/DC with daily updates and hundreds of active source portals; API surfaces include permit search/detail, property history, contractor profiles/search, status-transition events, saved searches/webhooks and coverage/platform statistics.
- Rare / undernoticed value: This is a potential hard-to-recreate multi-jurisdiction permit intelligence substrate rather than a one-city scraper. The SDK exposes project value, category/status, filed/issued/completed/expired dates, contractor/license, jurisdiction, geospatial fields and a limited structured enrichment layer for solar/roofing/new-construction. That can materially accelerate PermitPlate-style sales intelligence, construction-market signals and permit/regulatory research.
- Buyer / painful problem: Roofing/solar/HVAC/material suppliers, contractors, insurers, lenders, AEC vendors and permit-intelligence products need normalized project-start/status signals across thousands of incompatible city portals.
- Monetization / first paid wedge: Validate a narrow commercial vertical in 3–5 metros using permit events and contractor/property context; charge for filtered opportunity signals only after source coverage and update lag are independently measured.
- Build-time / data advantage: Very high. A genuinely maintained 100M-record, multi-portal normalized permit corpus could save many months to years of connector/data work.
- Evidence inspected: exact latest commit, whose message updates coverage to 783 active sources / 10,010 cities / 102M+ permits; README; 141 KB `openapi.json`; generated `PermitDetail.ts` and `PermitEnrichment.ts`; recursive SDK tree. The public schema exposes permit and event/search surfaces, but the returned `PermitDetail` model does not expose an immutable raw record, original portal URL or source hash, and only ~1–2% of permits are described as enriched. The OpenAPI header still carries older 93M+/8,000-city metadata, demonstrating documentation/version drift that must be measured rather than assumed away.
- Actual public license / rights: README identifies the SDK as Apache-2.0, but a root `LICENSE` file was not present at the inspected revision. The user’s standing assertion separately permits repository-owned code/content. The hosted PermitStack API, underlying municipal datasets, commercial service terms and any personal-data/privacy constraints are separate and are not covered by that assertion.
- Reuse classification: SDK/code can be used under the user’s standing permission; hosted data/service access requires separate terms. Do not ingest or monetize personal/private data; for commercial signals prefer project/jurisdiction/property/business facts that are lawfully public and necessary.
- Score: A5 / B5 / C5 / D5 / E3 / F3 = **26/30**. The moat is large, but evidence/provenance and hosted-data rights must be independently validated.
- Combination opportunities: PermitStack corpus + `michigan_data_permits_mcp` coverage-state semantics + CivicProof-style source-hash gate + PermitPlate entity/property resolution. Use it as a provider/benchmark, not as automatic proof of source completeness.
- Next action: Run a 100-permit, 5-jurisdiction provenance benchmark: compare API rows to official municipal records for recall, freshness, status-history fidelity, duplicate rate, source URL traceability and field-level conflicts before relying on it for customer decisions.

### jonathanleek/civic-data-warehouse — STRONG — 24/30
- URL: https://github.com/jonathanleek/civic-data-warehouse
- Exact revision: `54bd10f0b01610b4f5a1d46932ddf93d738f5e4d`
- Date inspected: 2026-09-19
- Category: Repository / Public-data ETL / Reusable Architecture
- Concrete capability: Active Apache Airflow/PostgreSQL civic-data warehouse that downloads St. Louis government data into a raw S3-style landing zone, dynamically stages files, normalizes to `current` schemas and maintains a separate `history` layer. Source families include parcel/assessor records, building/demolition/electrical/mechanical/occupancy/plumbing permits, property sales, inspections, condemnations/vacancies, public land and forestry data.
- Rare / undernoticed value: The commercially useful pattern is temporal public-data normalization: raw landing -> staging -> current canonical entities -> historical snapshots, backed by CI/DAG integrity tests. That is exactly the shape a permit/property intelligence product needs when source files are periodically replaced rather than versioned for the consumer.
- Buyer / painful problem: Permit/property intelligence vendors and municipal-data integrators need to unify parcel/building/address/legal-entity/permit/inspection data while retaining enough history to detect new permits, status changes and property-risk events.
- Monetization / first paid wedge: Use the architecture for one city/metro paid permit/property intelligence implementation, then generalize source-family adapters rather than treating every public CSV as a standalone feed.
- Build-time / data advantage: High; roughly 2–4 months of Airflow/source-landed/staging/current/history/data-model and data-quality architecture, even though the exact source URLs are St. Louis-specific.
- Evidence inspected: exact current commit; README architecture and source list; recursive tree with ingestion/staging DAGs, data dictionary, controlled vocabularies, normalized schema documentation and CI tests. Recent commits include a staging OOM/column-truncation fix and data-dictionary work, showing active operational hardening rather than a frozen demo.
- Actual public license / rights: No root `LICENSE` was found at the inspected revision. User’s standing assertion supplies separate commercial permission for repository-owned code/content. City/source datasets and personally identifying public-record fields retain their own legal/privacy/terms posture and must be treated separately.
- Reuse classification: Repository-owned implementation usable under the standing permission; external data rights/privacy remain source-specific.
- Score: A3 / B4 / C5 / D4 / E4 / F4 = **24/30**.
- Combination opportunities: Public portal/source adapter -> raw immutable landing/hash -> CDW-style normalized current/history entities -> PermitPlate business signals; add `building-permit-taxonomy`/coverage-state semantics and avoid storing unnecessary personal fields.
- Next action: Cleanly separate source snapshots from normalized history and benchmark one second municipality to see which parts of the schema generalize versus St. Louis-specific assumptions.

- Build-time / data advantage: Potentially high as a hosted data estate, but the rare server-side collectors and corpus are not present in this public repo and therefore were not verified from source.

The public GitHub artifact is primarily a remote-service client/documentation surface, so the core ingestion/evidence implementation remains unverified.
